strengths: Significance: The paper raises an important concern for bioimaging evaluation: strong benchmark scores may arise from low-level statistics, architectural priors, cell count, or tissue structure rather than biologically meaningful abstraction.

Originality: Combining random encoders, pixel statistics, structure-only cell graphs, layer-wise analysis, and natural-image controls across both Cell Painting and histopathology provides a useful diagnostic perspective. The HEST-1k-1NN construction and structure-only comparisons are particularly thought-provoking.

Soundness strengths: The evaluation covers multiple architectures, pretrained and untrained variants, intermediate layers, several biological datasets, three initialization seeds for random encoders, and patient-stratified HEST splits. The paper also reports extensive per-dataset and per-fold results.

The authors appropriately temper several findings: they acknowledge that structure performance may primarily reflect cell count, that prediction alignment does not establish shortcut use, and that private MAE backbones limit analysis. No material ethical concern is apparent because the study reuses existing benchmarks and makes no clinical-performance claim.
weaknesses: Soundness: Competitive simple baselines show that the evaluated tasks can be solved partly through simple signals; they do not establish the central claim that pretrained models fail to acquire high-level biological features. Such features may coexist with shortcut features or simply be irrelevant to these particular retrieval metrics. Likewise, moderately high correlations between model-induced rankings do not imply that models use essentially the same signal.

The strongest cell-culture evidence is narrow. RxRx3-core is reduced to ten images per gene without sufficient analysis of how this subsampling changes rankings or uncertainty, while the JUMP-CP experiment contains only eight ubiquitous positive-control compounds and primarily tests replicate identity. This is insufficient to support broad conclusions about microscopy representation learning.

The tissue interpretation remains substantially confounded by cell count. The paper itself shows strong agreement between graph-image and cell-count performance, and synthetic experiments only establish model capacity to detect arrangement—not that arrangement drives performance on real tissue. Structure extraction also relies on a pretrained CellViT segmenter, so this is not an entirely learning-free baseline.

Statistical evidence is weak for the breadth of comparisons: many HEST subsets contain only two patients, results are selected using the best model or best handcrafted configuration per dataset, and no paired significance tests or correction for extensive model/dataset/gene comparisons are reported. Fold standard deviations therefore do not resolve whether several highlighted differences are reliable.

Important implementation details remain underspecified, including RxRx3 fold and batch construction, image/profile aggregation and normalization, preprocessing of microscopy channels, ridge/PCA selection, and graph-training hyperparameters. There is no stated release of code or the new HEST-1k-1NN benchmark. Reliance on private MAE backbones further limits reproducibility, although this limitation is disclosed.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally understandable but sprawling, and several crucial results are relegated to dense, difficult-to-read appendix tables. There are also recurring proofreading and labeling problems, including inconsistent dataset names, malformed sentences, and a JUMP-CP figure caption that incorrectly refers to ImageNet retrieval.

The conclusions need tighter scope. The evidence convincingly diagnoses weaknesses of the selected metrics and datasets, but does not justify general statements about what current microscopy foundation models learn. This gap between benchmark critique and representation-level claims is decisive for the weak-reject rating.

strengths: The paper addresses an important question: whether microscopy benchmark scores reflect learned biological abstractions. Comparing RxRx3-core, JUMP-CP, HEST-1k, and ImageNet makes this potentially useful to both representation-learning and bioimaging communities.

The inclusion of pixel statistics, randomly initialized networks, cell-count features, and structure-only cell graphs is a valuable diagnostic contribution. In particular, the strong RxRx3-core performance of untrained ViTs and SingleConv, together with the similarity-ranking correlations, is a noteworthy empirical observation.

The evaluation is broader than the main text alone suggests: the appendices include intermediate-layer analyses, multiple architectures, initialization seeds, per-compound and per-gene results, synthetic structure experiments, and both original and coarsened HEST-1k evaluations.

The discussion is commendably more nuanced than the abstract. It acknowledges that in-domain models outperform the baselines on parts of JUMP-CP and HEST-1k, that proprietary MAE embeddings improve RxRx3-core recall by roughly 1.5 times, and that the apparent tissue-structure signal may largely reflect cell count.

No major ethical violation is apparent: the study reuses established datasets and does not make direct clinical deployment claims. The explicit acknowledgement of causal and interpretability limitations is a positive feature rather than a reason for rejection.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central claim that current models fail to acquire high-level biological features is not directly tested. Retrieval performance, layer-wise trends, and correlations between model rankings do not operationalize semantic abstraction or distinguish reliance on shortcuts from reliance on legitimate low-level biological morphology. Similar prediction rankings also do not establish that models use the same underlying signal.

The manuscript overgeneralizes mixed results. The strongest claim is driven mainly by RxRx3-core: on JUMP-CP, pretrained models consistently outperform untrained and pixel baselines; on HEST-1k-1NN, in-domain models substantially outperform structure-only models on most reported datasets; and the proprietary MAE models decisively improve RxRx3-core. These results support benchmark-specific cautions, not the broad conclusion stated in the abstract.

The RxRx3-core protocol is insufficiently controlled and documented for such strong conclusions. The authors replace the original dataset with three subsampled folds containing only ten images per gene, but do not fully specify fold construction, plate and batch stratification, channel normalization, profile aggregation, post-processing, or batch-effect correction. Consequently, it is unclear whether the surprising baseline performance reflects the benchmark, the altered protocol, or preprocessing choices.

The JUMP-CP experiment covers only eight shared positive-control compounds. Replicate retrieval for these conspicuous controls is a narrow task and does not support conclusions about chemical perturbation representations across the full dataset. Exact plate identities and fold assignments are also missing, limiting checks for laboratory or plate leakage.

The tissue analysis does not isolate spatial organization from cell count on real data. Figure 13 and Table 7 show that cell count is already extremely competitive, and the authors explicitly concede that count-conditioned or interventional analyses are needed. Synthetic classification only establishes model capacity; it does not show that real-tissue gains arise from organization. Moreover, HEST-1k-1NN changes resolution, smooths expression targets, and creates overlapping neighborhoods, so its results cannot straightforwardly diagnose the original benchmark.

Statistical support is weak. The paper repeatedly reports the best model across many architectures, layers, and preprocessing choices on the evaluation folds, without nested model selection, hypothesis tests, or multiplicity correction. Several HEST subsets contain only two patients, so fold-level standard deviations do not establish robust population-level differences.

Reproducibility is below the expected standard. There is no accompanying code or complete reproducibility statement; SingleConv is not specified precisely; training hyperparameters for the synthetic CNN/GNN experiments are absent; exact random seeds and split manifests are not provided; and multiple custom preprocessing and channel-expansion decisions are only partially described. Reliance on private pretrained backbones further limits part of the analysis, although the paper appropriately discloses this.

Presentation needs substantial revision. Several figures are crowded or too small, terminology is inconsistent, and Figure 23 incorrectly describes JUMP-CP compound retrieval as ImageNet retrieval. The manuscript would benefit from separating supported benchmark-specific findings from speculative interpretations.

Research-ethics treatment is minimal. Although the datasets are established and risks appear limited, the paper does not discuss dataset licenses, human-tissue governance, cohort bias, or the consequences of extrapolating these benchmark findings to biological or clinical use.

strengths: The paper provides a useful and fairly original diagnostic perspective on microscopy representation learning: untrained encoders, pixel statistics, cell counts, and structure-only cell graphs make benchmark scores substantially more interpretable than comparisons among pretrained models alone.

The empirical scope is broad, spanning RxRx3-core, a five-fold JUMP-CP subset, HEST-1k and the proposed HEST-1k-1NN variant, plus ImageNet-1k as a reference. Intermediate-layer analyses and comparisons across in-domain, out-of-domain, and untrained models are especially informative.

Several results are compelling and practically significant. On RxRx3-core, untrained ViTs and SingleConv are competitive with several pretrained models and induce similar gene-pair rankings; on JUMP-CP and HEST, the experiments also identify settings where in-domain pretraining provides clear gains. This nuanced picture is more valuable than a blanket negative conclusion.

The evaluation includes useful robustness evidence: three initializations for untrained models, multiple folds, per-compound JUMP-CP results, gene-wise HEST comparisons, and extensive appendix tables. The synthetic point-set study also verifies that the proposed structural representations can encode organization beyond cell count in a controlled setting.

The authors discuss important limitations candidly, including the inability of prediction alignment to establish shortcut use, the possible dominance of cell count in tissue experiments, and the restricted analysis of proprietary MAE models. No material ethical concern is apparent because the study reuses established biological-image benchmarks and does not make clinical claims.
weaknesses: The strongest semantic claim is not fully established. Competitive untrained or structure-only baselines show that simple signals are sufficient for a benchmark, but do not demonstrate that pretrained models fail to learn biologically meaningful high-level features or that they actually use the same shortcut. Similar gene-ranking correlations likewise do not identify the causal information used by each model.

The RxRx3 comparison is insufficiently controlled for embedding dimension, aggregation, normalization, and architecture-specific feature geometry. The PCA analysis is correlational; a stronger test would dimension-match representations and evaluate learned models after removing or conditioning on pixel statistics, cell count, batch, and other candidate confounders. A standard CellProfiler morphology baseline would also strengthen the calibration.

The tissue interpretation remains uncertain on real data. The paper itself shows strong agreement between structure-only predictions and cell count, yet does not condition on count while comparing arrangements. HEST-1k-1NN additionally changes scale and smooths transcriptomic targets, making it easier and altering model rankings; several constituent datasets contain only two patients, limiting the strength and generality of conclusions drawn from fold-level variation.

The JUMP-CP benchmark contains only eight shared positive-control compounds. This supports a focused diagnostic study but is too narrow to justify broad conclusions about chemical-perturbation representation learning, particularly because some compounds are nearly trivial and others show no detectable phenotype.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Public datasets, model identifiers, splits, and many construction details are supplied, but there is no accompanying code release, and important implementation details—especially batch-effect mitigation, image/profile aggregation, preprocessing, and optimization or hyperparameters for trained structural models—are underspecified. Some evaluated proprietary backbones are unavailable, although the authors appropriately disclose this.

Presentation is generally understandable but needs polishing: several figures are dense, Figure 3 labels its vertical axis as recall while describing mAP, Figure 23 incorrectly refers to ImageNet retrieval for JUMP-CP compounds, and numerous grammatical or typographical errors remain. These issues do not overturn the contribution but impede precise interpretation.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a timely and consequential question—whether microscopy benchmarks measure learned biological abstractions—and derives useful recommendations such as reporting pixel, cell-count, and untrained-network baselines alongside conventional scores.

Soundness: The empirical scope is substantial, covering cell-culture retrieval, spatial-transcriptomics prediction, cancer subtyping, natural-image controls, intermediate layers, multiple random initializations, and both image- and graph-based encoders. Several conclusions are appropriately nuanced; for example, in-domain models clearly outperform baselines on parts of JUMP-CP and HEST-1k.

Originality: Applying untrained encoders and structure-only tissue representations jointly across biological scales provides a useful diagnostic perspective, even though the individual baseline ideas are not new.

Presentation: Per-compound, per-gene, layer-wise, and ranking-correlation analyses expose behavior hidden by aggregate metrics. The discussion candidly acknowledges that prediction alignment does not prove shortcut use and that cell count may explain the tissue results.

Reproducibility and ethics: Most datasets, model configurations, splits, and preprocessing choices are documented in extensive appendices, with seed/fold variability reported for several experiments. The study uses public, previously released data and raises no material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: Similar performance or correlated rankings between pretrained and untrained models shows that a benchmark can be solved without learned semantics, but it does not establish that pretrained models lack high-level biological representations or exploit the same shortcuts. The paper acknowledges this limitation, yet the title, abstract, and statements that architectural bias can 'dominate' performance remain broader than the evidence supports.

The main RxRx3-core evidence relies on a materially altered protocol: only 10 images per gene are retained despite the original dataset containing roughly 50–9,450, the bottom similarity tail is removed, and a new three-fold procedure is introduced. These choices may disproportionately discard gains from learned representations, and there is no sensitivity analysis over replicate count or direct evaluation under the complete canonical protocol sufficient to establish robustness of the central result.

The tissue interpretation is not adequately identified. Structure-only graph performance is strongly aligned with cell count, and the manuscript explicitly concedes that it does not show arrangement rather than count drives performance on real tissue. Conditioning or matching on cell count is needed before characterizing spatial organization as a strong independent modality.

Statistical support is limited. Many comparisons involve three folds, datasets with only two patients, selection of the best model or handcrafted transformation, and overlapping uncertainty, but no paired tests or confidence intervals for the claimed pretrained-versus-baseline equivalences are provided. Variability from preprocessing, segmentation, and benchmark construction is also insufficiently assessed.

The evaluation is selective: JUMP-CP uses only eight positive-control compounds, HEST-1k-1NN smooths expression targets while introducing overlapping coarsened patches, and some headline comparisons report best-in-class models rather than uniformly paired architectures. These design choices are informative diagnostics but do not justify conclusions about microscopy representation learning broadly.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the stated code release: the manuscript contains a code footnote marker without an accessible URL, and key implementation details such as training hyperparameters for synthetic graph models and some aggregation/normalization settings are deferred to external implementations. Private MAE backbones also prevent the proposed layer-wise analysis of the strongest RxRx3 models.

Presentation would benefit from substantial tightening. The 45-page manuscript contains many small, dense figures, grammatical errors, inconsistent terminology, and occasional table/caption ambiguities, making the central evidential chain harder to follow. The impact statement is generic and does not discuss possible harms from overinterpreting biological benchmark predictions.

strengths: The paper asks an important question for bioimaging: whether benchmark scores reflect learned biological abstractions or signals available to simple baselines. Including pixel statistics, CellProfiler features, random encoders, cell count, and structure-only representations is useful benchmarking practice with practical significance.
The empirical scope is substantial, spanning RxRx3-core, JUMP-CP, JUMP-MoA, HEST-1k, BRACS, BACH, and ImageNet, with several model families and both intermediate-layer and final-layer evaluations.

Several analyses are informative beyond aggregate leaderboards, including per-compound and per-gene breakdowns, correlations between gene-pair rankings, comparisons across network depth, and experiments over multiple random initializations.

The paper reports important counterevidence to its most pessimistic narrative: in-domain models clearly outperform simple baselines on parts of JUMP-CP and HEST-1k, and the proprietary MAE embeddings substantially improve RxRx3 retrieval. This makes the empirical account more balanced.

Most datasets and evaluated models are public, patient-level splits are used for tissue experiments, and the authors promise code release. The limitations section candidly states that prediction alignment does not establish shortcut use and that tissue-structure performance may largely reflect cell count.

The work raises no major new ethical concern. Its emphasis on cautious interpretation of biomedical benchmarks is beneficial, although downstream biological or clinical claims would still require independent validation.
weaknesses: Soundness: Competitive performance by an untrained or ablated baseline does not establish that a trained model lacks high-level biological features or uses the same shortcut. A representation can contain both simple and biological signals while the selected probe, aggregation, labels, or metric only rewards the former. Spearman agreement between similarity rankings is suggestive but does not identify the causal features used. This gap directly affects the paper's central claims about what models 'really learn.'

Soundness: The main RxRx3 protocol substantially modifies the published benchmark by retaining only 10 images per gene, using three newly constructed folds, and discarding the bottom similarity tail. The manuscript does not adequately establish that conclusions under this heavily subsampled protocol generalize to the original evaluation. Figure 18 shows full-dataset results, but the principal layer-wise, seed, and ranking analyses center on the altered version.

Soundness: The PCA-collapse argument is inadequately controlled. Variance explained by the first two components depends on representation dimension, scaling, architecture, pooling, and preprocessing; these factors differ considerably across ResNets, ViTs, pixel features, and SingleConv. Correlation with retrieval performance therefore does not support the proposed explanatory interpretation without dimension matching, whitening controls, or intervention experiments.

Soundness: Statistical evidence is weak for several prominent comparisons. HEST subsets such as PRAD, SKCM, and COAD contain only two patients; results select the best model separately for each dataset and modality from many candidates, yet provide no correction for this selection, paired tests, or confidence intervals over independent patients. Fold standard deviations do not resolve the very small effective sample size.

Soundness: The structure-only tissue results do not demonstrate that spatial arrangement, rather than cell count or segmentation artifacts, drives performance. Centroids come from a learned CellViT segmentation system, and the authors' own real-data analysis shows strong alignment with an engineered cell-count baseline. Synthetic classification only establishes model capacity on artificial patterns, not use of analogous structure in real tissue. The manuscript acknowledges this honestly, but it substantially limits the claimed contribution.

Significance and originality: Strong simple baselines and warnings about biological benchmark confounding are valuable, but both are already well motivated by the cited literature. The paper does not propose a validated new benchmark, a causal diagnostic, or a correction method. Its new structure-only view is interesting, yet the real-data evidence cannot separate organization from count, leaving the main advance primarily as a broad empirical caution.

Reproducibility: Important implementation details are deferred to external pipelines or remain underspecified, including the exact SingleConv construction, fold-generation and sampling seeds, control normalization and profile aggregation, input normalization and channel-expansion details, synthetic/GNN training hyperparameters, and model-selection rules. The best RxRx3 MAE backbones are private, preventing the layer-wise analysis that motivates much of the paper.

Presentation: The manuscript is overly broad and places many necessary results in a long appendix while key main-text conclusions rely on dense, difficult-to-read plots rather than numerical tables. There are also numerous typographical and labeling problems, including a Recall axis for an mAP figure, Figure 26 incorrectly describing ImageNet retrieval, inconsistent SKCM/SCKM naming, duplicated words, and incomplete sentences. These issues materially hinder verification.

Overall, the baseline study contains useful observations, but the evidence supports the narrower conclusion that current metrics can sometimes be solved by simple signals—not the broader conclusion that the evaluated models fail to acquire biologically meaningful abstractions. The central causal interpretation, altered benchmark protocol, weak statistical treatment, and incomplete reproducibility require substantial revision before the work can be reliably built upon.

strengths: Soundness: The paper evaluates a notably broad set of controls—pixel statistics, CellProfiler features, randomly initialized CNNs/ViTs, cell count, and structure-only graphs—across RxRx3-core, JUMP-CP/JUMP-MoA, HEST-1k, breast-cancer datasets, and an ImageNet reference. Multiple seeds or folds are reported for several principal experiments, and layer-wise, per-compound, per-gene, ranking-correlation, and dimensionality analyses generally support the qualitative conclusions.

Significance: Demonstrating that untrained ViTs and even SingleConv can approach pretrained models on RxRx3-core is an important warning for microscopy representation evaluation. The practical recommendations—report strong uninformed baselines, layer-wise behavior, and granular diagnostic breakdowns—could materially improve future benchmarks.

Originality: The individual baselines are simple and related phenomena are known, but assembling them into a cross-scale audit of microscopy benchmarks provides useful new understanding. The structure-only tissue analysis is especially thought-provoking.

Presentation: The manuscript is well organized, visually clear, and unusually candid about mixed results. It explicitly shows tasks where in-domain pretraining helps, such as selected JUMP-CP compounds and HEST subsets, rather than forcing a uniformly negative narrative.

The discussion appropriately limits causal interpretation: it acknowledges that prediction alignment does not prove models use the same shortcuts and that tissue results may largely reflect cell count rather than spatial arrangement.

Reproducibility and ethics: Datasets, model identifiers, layer choices, folds, metrics, and many preprocessing details are documented extensively; major resources are public. The impact statement appropriately warns that benchmark performance is not a substitute for preclinical safety and efficacy validation.
weaknesses: Soundness: The strongest rhetoric about failure to learn “high-level biological abstractions” is not directly established. Competitive random features show that a benchmark can be solved without learned semantics, but do not prove that a pretrained model lacks such semantics or uses the same shortcut. Similarity of pairwise rankings and PCA dimensionality remains correlational, as the authors partly acknowledge.

The RxRx3-core headline analysis modifies the benchmark substantially: it subsamples only 10 images per gene, uses three constructed folds, and drops the bottom similarity tail. These choices may alter biological signal-to-noise and the relative advantage of low-level features. Figure 18 partially addresses the full benchmark, but the full-data protocol and uncertainty are not analyzed as thoroughly as the modified setting.

The tissue conclusions rest heavily on small HEST subsets—PRAD and COAD each contain only two patients—and often compare the best model selected separately for each dataset/modality. Without nested model selection, uncertainty over this selection process, or statistical tests, apparently competitive differences may be optimistic.

The paper does not isolate spatial arrangement from cell count on real tissue. Figure 17 and the authors’ own analysis suggest that count is a dominant correlate; synthetic tasks establish model capacity but not that real-tissue gains arise from organization. Consequently, the claimed value of “structure-only” representations is better supported than the more specific interpretation involving spatial organization.

Several evaluations are narrow or exploratory: JUMP-CP uses only eight positive-control compounds, JUMP-MoA has 43 two-compound classes, and breast-cancer results report the best patchification/aggregation choice. Broader held-out perturbations and prespecified selection rules would strengthen generality.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the detailed appendix: the manuscript says code is released, but the displayed PDF provides no usable repository link or footnote target. Some consequential details—exact fold construction, normalization/batch-correction pipeline, hyperparameter selection, and evaluation code for newly constructed datasets—are deferred to prior implementations rather than fully specified.

Presentation could be tightened: there are numerous grammatical/typographical errors, inconsistent names such as SKCM/SCKM and H-Optimus capitalization, and some tables report standard deviations inconsistently. These do not obscure the main message but fall short of a polished final version.
